Theme of the month: It’s YOUR club!
Paraphrasing John Kennedy: “Ask not what your
Guild can do for you. Ask what you can do for your
Guild!”
At the time of writing this I, and a horde of our
members, have just returned from Portland and we
are all abuzz with excitement. Too bad we can’t
have the Symposium in Vancouver. Thank you to
Kevin Melanson for establishing our “whatsapp”
group. The AP certainly helped us coordinate
matters during a hectic but awesome weekend. Kudos to Cathy Friesen for volunteering in the member registration booth and similarly to Art Liestman
for demonstrating therming and texturing at the
event (and for giving me a ride there and back). I
am sure there were others that donated their time
– well done!
Dan & Yolanda have again offered their park setting
should someone wish to organize a picnic. Maybe
there is something else on the horizon for us to partake in.
Thank you to the dozen of us that donated their
time and effort at the PoMo Art Shuffle! In no particular order, thank you to Bill Fowle, Tracy Hill, Pippa Lattey, David Adolf, Dennis Houle, Brian Lunt,
Alan Jones, Dan Breck, Chris Stiles, Claudia Hayward, Bob James, and especially Bruce Campbell for
putting it all together. Also a big thanks to Bill &
Tracy, Brian, Dan for helping the following day to
run the GVWG Flea Market / Auction. It was not
particularly well attended but people seemed to
have fun. Maybe the fair weather was to blame?
Some people got some rather good deals and it was
fun to see some fierce bidding wars on a couple of
the big ticket items and just about everyone won a
door prize. Thank you also to: Scott Belway, Matt
Low, Phil Winch for your tool donations and a massive, massive thanks to Bob Gadd of Woodworkers
Specialties for his generous donations.
There is no President’s Challenge for next meeting!
However, Pippa is championing the collaboration
project where pairs of members can exchange an
unfinished piece and work on it over the summer
and bring the finished piece in for the September
meeting.
Steve

June 2024
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 4
The first documented history of woodturning dates
back to the 3rd century BC. By the 13th century AD
more information became available and since the
mid part of the last century, information about
woodturning, and especially safety and health issues, has exploded. Worldwide, much has been
written about the safety and health risks for
woodturners. If you ‘Google’ the topic you get over
five million hits. Notwithstanding, The Greater Vancouver Woodturners Guild Newsletter has covered
this subject well over the years. If you go to
www.gvwg.ca you will find on the left hand side of
the home page the subject - Safety. (editor’s note:
The Safety link is now on the menu bar just below
the banner) It provides a wide range of references
including the American Association of Woodturners
web page which also has many useful references.
However, it is a new year and a reminder that we
can enjoy woodturning as long as we are mindful
of the dangers, to be able to avoid accidents and
remain healthy, is not a bad idea.
Yes, there are many guidelines published by many
experts, guilds, associations and individual turners
on safety in the workshop. When you read all this
you wonder if you should be woodturning at all. If
you follow everything that is recommended your
work shop will be dysfunctional and if you wear all
the safety equipment recommended you will be
immobile and, in fact, a safety risk! However, it is
not OK to be light hearted in these things because,
be assured, injury and death have occurred to our
colleagues while woodturning. We all have stories
of being cut by our tools, sustaining a bruise or
abrasion while preparing our wood or having aches
and pains while in an awkward, sustained position.
In the March 2008 issue of our newsletter, a guild
member tells us he had the tendons of his right
hand severed when a bowl he was turning flew off
the lathe. This required extensive surgery and prolonged rehabilitation. I am not sure if he has been
left with a residual disability and whether or not he
has been able to return to turning. We have seen
the evidence of other serious injuries in our colleagues such as facial scars caused by a stray piece
of wood or wood chip because of not wearing a full
face shield. There are many stories of ‘near misses’
which should not be happening!
Thank goodness fatalities in woodturning are rare
but it does occur. I was told of an individual who
was using his grinder to sharpen his gouge when
the grinding wheel blew up and with tremendous
force hit him in the chest causing death. In the August 2011 issue of the American Woodturner, Journal of the American Association of Woodturners,
appeared a memoriam for woodturner, Joan
Gilmer Kelly, an experienced and very talented
woodturner. Ms. Kelly died on May 17, 2011 as a
result of an accident that occurred while she was
turning wood. In this memoriam there was no
mention of the cause of how such a horrific accident occurred so I took the opportunity to call the
AAW. The representative I spoke to advised that
her family did not wish this information made public and, therefore, out of respect I will not speculate. I was referred to the web site of her guild, The
Mid-South Woodturners Guild (MSWG), Memphis,
TN. Since this tragic accident the MSWG has developed a Lathe Safety Check List which they recommend every woodturner print out, laminate, and
hang near the lathe in a “clearly visible position”.
Safety in woodturning is not a subject to be taken
lightly. If you operate mechanized equipment such
as a lathe and all the other equipment involved in
turning wood, it is imperative that safety be your
(Continued on page 5)
This article is reprinted from the January 2012
GVWG Newsletter.

June 2024
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 5
first priority. Please spend time to familiarize yourself with some of the many publications available
through the GVWG web site and other resources
through the internet. In researching this article I
reviewed multiple papers and guidelines. The Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety
(www.ccohs.ca), Canada’s national resource for
occupational health and safety, has guidelines for
woodturning lathes as does numerous associations
and woodturning guilds throughout the world. A
summary of the recommendations that they all
have in common is as follows:
• Always wear an approved face shield when
turning – not eye protection alone
• Have proper work shop ventilation
• Always use respiratory protection, especially
when sanding
• Do not wear jewelry or loose clothing and always tie back long hair
• Ensure your equipment is regularly maintained
and in good working order
• Ensure the electrical components are working
properly and there are no sparks
• Ensure there are no oily rags or excessive
shavings or debris which could be a fire risk
• Always keep your work area clean and free of
clutter
• Always work with sharp tools
• Ensure your blank is securely mounted
• Always rotate the blank by hand, one full rotation, before turning on the lathe
• Always check lathe speed before turning on
your lathe
• Always follow lathe speed guidelines (the diameter of the blank in inches times the lathe
speed should be between 6000 and 9000
rpm)
• Start with a slow speed and increase according
to the guidelines when the work piece is balanced
• Always stop your lathe before adjusting the
tool rest
• Use the tool for what it was designed for; use
the right tool for the right task
• Never leave your lathe turning unattended
There are many health risks in turning wood and
there is much written about it, especially wood
dust and respiratory disease. All wood dust is a primary irritant to the respiratory tract and will cause
nasal and lung irritation depending on the particle
size. Those with pre-existing lung disease, such as
chronic obstructive lung disease, are at greater risk
for aggravation of their condition if exposed to
wood dust. Wood dust can cause drying and irritation of the skin and aggravate pre-existing skin conditions such as eczema. Wood dust will also cause
eye irritation and if you wear contacts the dust particle can get under the lens and cause a corneal
abrasion. Some wood contains resins and other
substances which are called sensitizers and will
cause an allergic reaction when you are exposed,
especially with repeated or prolonged exposure.
On the GVWG website you will find an excellent
overview of wood toxicity with a list of woods and
a ranking of potential health risks for the skin and
respiratory system. Exposure to fine particulate
wood dust from trees that are known to be sensitizers such as Western Red Cedar and teak can
cause asthma. If you develop asthma you then become more susceptible for primary lung irritation
or ‘twitchy airways’ when exposed to general ambient dust, thus putting you at risk for having to
give up woodturning altogether. Apart from primary wood dusts some woods contain fungus known
as spalting. Fungus can cause infection or allergic
reaction. In a recent GVWG newsletter a colleague
told us about his development of maple bark disease caused by the fungal spores of Cryptostroma
corticale, which caused an allergic lung condition.
As a result he had to stop woodturning after many
years and sell all his equipment.
In 1997 the International Agency for Research on
Cancer (IARC – world recognized scientific expertise on cancer) declared all wood dust to be a
Group 1 carcinogen to humans. This means that
there is sufficient scientific evidence that chronic
exposure to high levels of any wood dust, not just
(Continued from page 4)
(Continued on page 6)

June 2024
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 6
hardwood, will cause nasosinus cancer. This cancer
has a long latency – time from exposure to disease
– meaning that from the time of exposure you may
not develop the cancer for 15 to 30 years. You may
have had high exposure for several years and then
took measures to minimize your exposure but that
does not mitigate the risk of possible cancer years
from now. Therefore, right from the beginning of
woodturning, eliminate or reduce to as low as reasonably possible any exposure to wood dust. A
workshop dust collection system and a personal
respirator are critical to reducing your exposure.
There is much discussion about the various types of
dust collection systems, the bottom line is, try to
collect dust before it becomes airborne. As this is
difficult to do, always wear a respirator when exposed to fine dust particulates. There are many
types of respirators ranging from a paper mask to a
full face unit with filtered air. At the very least a
good paper mask should be used, preferably an
N95 type mask to ensure that fine particulates are
captured.
Don’t forget that other things we use in the course
of turning and finishing can cause skin and respiratory health problems. Things that we use on a regular basis such as cyanoacrylate (CA) glues, oils,
pigments, formaldehyde containing substances and
many more are known sensitizers and primary irritants. They can cause allergic or irritant dermatitis
and solvents can cause neurological problems. Aniline dyes, used for coloring wood, is a known carcinogen and will cause kidney cancer. When using
these substances always use in a well ventilated
area and use respiratory and skin protection.
There are other health concerns related to
woodturning. Physical health risk factors are also
very important. Good body posture is often difficult
to achieve with woodturning as we often find ourselves in an awkward, sustained bending forward
position. This can cause muscle strain in the neck
and back muscles. As we get older we are all prone
to degenerative changes in our spine and such
awkward postures will aggravate our spine and
cause pain. This can be a distraction for us when
turning and for some individuals with significant
arthritis of the spine may cause them to give up
turning all together. Most woodturners turn standing (although smaller lathes will allow for sitting)
and this can cause discomfort for those with hip,
knee or ankle conditions. If you hold your hand
tools too tightly or in awkward positions for a sustained period of time you could develop wrist and
forearm tendonitis or carpel tunnel syndrome (a
condition affecting the nerves of the hand and fingers). In preparation for turning do a few warm-up
exercises to prepare them for the tasks you require
of them. Do not turn for long periods without taking a break and do a few stretches for your arms,
legs and back. Being physically fit is not only good
for a long life but it also prepares you for
woodturning for as long as you wish.
Noise is a physical risk to your hearing. When exposed for a prolonged period to noisy equipment
use hearing protection. Ear plugs or ear muffs with
industrial standard certification should be worn.
Some full face respirators incorporate hearing protection in their design. A rule of thumb is – if you
have to shout to have someone hear you when the
equipment is running, it is too loud and hearing
protection should be worn.
It is critical that you maintain good mental and
emotional health if you plan to turn wood. You are
working with dangerous, moving equipment and
focus and concentration is paramount to being safe
and working safely. A lapse in your concentration
can be fatal. Therefore, do not turn if you are tired.
There will always be another day. Do not turn if
you have had alcohol or any drug that can impair
your cognitive function and delay your reflex response. This includes the use of opiate drugs such
as Tylenol with Codeine. Other types of prescribed
drugs such as antidepressants, anti-anxiety drugs
or sleeping pills are very common and should be
used with caution. Generally, if you have been prescribed one of these types of drugs it will take 4 to
6 weeks for your body to ‘acclimatize’ to the side
effects, then you should be OK. However, there are
many types of drugs with many side effects and the
best thing is to discuss the safety risks with your
doctor before you start turning after taking them.
(Continued from page 5)
(Continued on page 7)

June 2024
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 7
It goes without saying that street drugs including
marijuana should never be used. Apart from being
illegal (in 2012 - ed.) they will impair cognitive function such as decision making and cause reflex delay. Studies have shown that these effects can last
up to 72 hours after use.
Your mental state or mood can impact your ability
to turn safely. Do not turn if you are depressed,
angry or anxious. Your concentration will be affected and that is when accidents occur. If you are having a ‘bad day’ and the woodturning is just not going as it should, stop, have a break, or leave your
project for another day. You will find that things
will get better.
Do not allow yourself to be distracted while your
lathe is running and you are turning. Teach your
family and friends about the dangers involved so
they will not distract or surprise you when you are
turning.
Lastly, remember about the safety and health of
the user of the piece that you have turned. Be sure
to use finishes that will be appropriate for its use,
do not use toxic finishes if the piece is designed to
hold food. Be mindful how the piece will be handled to ensure it will not be a physical hazard to
the end user, for example, a toy for a small child.
In conclusion, woodturning is an enjoyable hobby
and for some, an enjoyable profession. If we practice good common sense, know our tools, know the
risks associated with their use and use them safely,
the occurrence of accidents, injuries and illness will
be minimized. I encourage you to always think
about safety and health as you enter your workshop, have a safety checklist to review before you
get started, maintain good health practices and
you will enjoy your craft for as long as you choose.
(Continued from page 6)
This Weed Pot is a piece of walnut 7” diameter x 8”
tall, turned end grain, and then was sealed and
stored in my shop for about two years. I acquired
this walnut from an acquaintance who requested
that I remove his whole tree. BINGO. After returning it, the stone, bulrush and green brush work
were carved out using a Master-carver Micro-pro
with various burrs. A horizontal line was burnt in
with copper wire to separate the stone from brush.
The finish applied is walnut oil and an assortment
of acrylic paints dry brushed on. The interior was
hollowed out using the “Simply Hollowing System”
which employs an articulating arm. There exists a
bit of fine cracking at the bottom so this embellishing hides this well. Should I do this again maybe the
greenery could protrude out a bit and hang over
the rockery some what for a different effect.

We have all been there. You put your battery pack
in the charger and it does not recharge.
What has happened is your pack has discharged
enough that it is now in a sleep mode that the
charger will not revive.
I have been volunteering at a Repair Café for the
past 5 years and have fixed lots of batteries and
kept them from the landfill.
Chargers not able to recognize low voltage batteries is the issue. Not sure if this is a manufacturer’s
marketing trick to make you buy a new battery
pack (?) but this following method could save you
some bucks so you can buy other turning tools and
save your battery.
First: Make sure your terminals are clean. They
may be dirty or rusty because you are turning lots
of wet green wood. Just buff them up with some
sandpaper or clean them up with an alcohol wipe.
Second: You can try to wake your battery up from
sleep mode by using another battery or better still
using a DC power source like one from the many
wall chargers you have stuffed in a drawer somewhere.
Remember when you do the wired connections,
you want to be able to connect and disconnect easily ! You must have the correct polarity as well.
Connect the positive contact on one of the batteries to the positive contact on the other battery or
DC power source
Then do the same thing, but with the negative contacts. Make sure you get this right as getting it
wrong could cause damage to your battery.
Once you have connected this, leave them connected for a few seconds then disconnect one end
of the negative contacts.
You may have to do this several times depending
on the battery condition or manufacturer.
Some batteries only need a few “hits” or mini
(Continued on page 9)

June 2024
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 9
boosts, then they start showing a small 6 volt
charge. This pushes the battery out of sleep mode.
Now its time to put it into its regular charger and
let it charge normally.
I have found that some batteries take much longer
to revive than others.
I made my own “Battery CPR Unit” for use at Repair Café. Inside I have a 12v DC power pack for the
low voltage contact that goes to the battery. It is all
powered by a 120v input.
It has low voltage output alligator
clamp leads to grab onto positive
and
negative
exposed
blade
battery contacts on some battery
styles.
I also have adaptor inserts for
the battery packs that the contacts are buried inside the housing.
A momentary-on toggle switch makes it easy for
anyone in our Repair Café to safely use the device
and not leave it on too long.
By using an electrical meter you can watch your
progress and see the battery gaining voltage.
For other articles on different style battery revivals,
check out some past GVWG Newsletter articles like
in the July/August and September 2020 issues !

I’ve written this article for a couple reasons… to
share my limited knowledge with others, and just
as importantly, so that I could remember how to
use the jig the next time I try. I built this jig 2 years
ago, used it a few times, and then went to use it
again a few days ago, but couldn’t remember how.
I knew there was a spreadsheet involved to calculate the angles and markings on the blank, but I
searched my Excel files and could not find it. I
knew there was a video, but couldn’t find that either, and couldn’t even remember the gentleman’s
name who produced the spreadsheet and video.
After many Google searches, Gavin’s name popped
up, and I learned that it was a Google Sheet, not an
Excel sheet on my computer, so I was able to get to
work.
Here are some links to videos, the Google Sheet,
and drawings:
•
The Angle Finder Jig VII in Action - https://
www.youtube.com/watch?v=ppbcVUdDAIc
•
Making The Angle Finder Jig VII -
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hKYdwELDNI
•
The previous video briefly mentions an earlier
version VI of the jig, which is more of a manual
operation, not using the google sheet. I prefer
the VII jig, but this video explains the use of the
version VI for those who don’t want to bother
with the Google sheet. https://
www.youtube.com/watch?v=hYahys3dd1o
•
The Google Sheet - https://docs.google.com/
spreadsheets/
d/10wnNTGQ9Y1REO1udz6rXNcLwwpyYR7Kn1
QBS1DwGqDk/edit#gid=389075054
•
Drawings of the components to make the jig
(drafted to scale by someone else) https://
drive.google.com/file/
d/1w8JYGTHiSu05BP_i9rNJ50ZhjDdpMnch/
view
•
If you have a 3D printer, this video, by “The
Grain Doctor” gives an overview of 3D printing
and using the jig. https://www.youtube.com/
watch?v=QViwRjm0dYc
•
And this website probably provides all the necessary 3-D settings. https://
www.thingiverse.com/thing:3366592 ( I wasn’t
able to download and open any of the files,
since I don’t have the required software….anyone with a 3D printer probably does)
So, after viewing the videos, if you’re interested in
making your own jig, here’s how I approached it.
The video explains how to make the jig in great detail, using a compass, drawing tangent lines, etc.
But you can save some drafting time by printing
out the 3 drawings noted above.
•
The first one is full size, so it can be printed as
is to trace out on Plexiglas (Gavin refers to Perspex in his video - it’s the same stuff). This
drawing is also used to make the spacer, but
the 2 holes are not drilled, nor is it necessary to
cut the 2 notches in the side.
•
The protractor is scale 1:1.88, print to default
settings, cut out the protractor section only,
and lay it on your scanner, set your printer to
enlarge 188%, copy and extend the straight
section with a ruler. You may need to tweak
the enlarge settings until you get an exact full
size drawing. The critical measurements are
109 mm and 90 mm radius. Or you can follow
the steps in Gavin’s video to make your own
full size drawing.
•
The triangle pointer is scale 1:1.58 so set your
printer to enlarge 158% and print, and check to
ensure the dimensions are correct.
After cutting out the 4 components, double check
the radiuses of your McNaughton blades. Draw
the radiuses 89mm, 136mm, 176mm and 275mm
on paper, and lay your blades on top to ensure
they match (these are center line of blade radius).
Two of mine didn’t, and through trial and error
(Continued on page 11)

June 2024
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 11
with a compass, I determined that mine were
82mm and 126mm. I suspect that was because of
years of mis-use, forcing the cut and bending the
bars slightly, or McNaughton changed their design.
As a result, the first few bowls I cored were quite a
bit shallower than they should have been, resulting
in a useless inner bowl. As soon as I corrected the
radiuses in the Google sheet, my bowls were closer
to the predicted depth.
If your blades are ok, then proceed, if not, then you
will need to follow Gavin’s instructions for the triangle pointer, draw the correct arcs, and tangent
lines, which will shift the holes minimally. And,
change the radiuses in the Google sheet.
Be very careful that the drill bit doesn’t drift when
drilling the holes. Mark the center points with a
centre punch, use a drill press, drill a small pilot
hole, and then drill full size holes. Use an awl to
scribe the line on the triangle pointer.
Two things I did differently. I used a jig saw, not a
coping saw to cut the arcs, after drilling two 6mm
holes at each end. And I didn’t burn the degree
points. I tried on a scrap piece, made a mess, so I
tried a different method. I printed out the full size
protractor portion of the drawing onto photo paper, (heavy paper might work as well) and glued it
to the underside of Plexiglas with thin CA glue. I
trimmed the sheet down a bit, taped it in place
along the bottom edge with masking tape, being
careful to ensure that the 0 point was perpendicular to the hole in the base line, glued the arc section, and trimmed the excess after the glue had
set. The CA glue made it a bit blotchy, as you can
see in the photo…..but it works. (Clear epoxy glue
might work better, experiment on a scrap piece
before gluing to the actual protractor.)
How to use Gavin’s Google sheet and make it your
own. You will note that it is View only, which
means you can’t enter any blank dimensions or
wall thicknesses in the Inputs section.
To use this sheet, you will have to make your own
copy. Click on File then in the next screen, click on
Make a copy. That is the copy that you can use,
and keep for future use. Play around with it a bit
and you will notice that any change in any of the
Inputs section will change the Results section. It’s
all magic, complex formulas at work in the background. DO NOT enter any numbers in the Results
section above the blue circle or you will destroy the
formulas (except you must change the blade radiuses if yours are different).
If you’re not familiar with spreadsheets….to change
the blade radius, move your mouse pointer to the
current radius, click to highlight, and type in a new
radius, then Enter. Same procedure to edit the Inputs section for diameter, depth, wall and bottom
thickness. To change the choice of blade, click on
the down arrow, and a drop down menu will ap-
(Continued from page 10)
(Continued on page 12)

June 2024
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 12
pear, click on the one you want. And did I mention??? Don’t type anything in the Results section
above the blue circle
Note that in the screen shot, the 4th cut indicates a
cut angle of 64 degrees. But the protractor only
goes to + or – 60 degrees. So that 4th cut is not
possible. However, change the bottom thickness
to 6%, all the angles change, and that 4th bowl will
have a cut angle of 53 degrees. That said, I’d want
to gain a lot of experience using this jig before
cutting the bottom thickness that thin, if you want
to put a foot on the bowl. That doesn’t leave much
margin of error. (I’ve never attempted nested
bowls with dry wood, I only core wet, and use 10%
wall and 8% bottom thickness). Change the wall
thickness to 10% and bottom to 10% and you will
see that only 2 bowls can be cut, #3 & #4 cut angles
change to 67 & 112 degrees respectively. Change
the bottom to 8% and now you can get 3 bowls.
The other bit of information in this Google sheet is
the Blade plunge circumference. That is how far
the blade will plunge into the bowl blank until it
reaches the centre. So although it’s not necessary,
I find it helpful to measure along the radius of the
blade and mark the blade with masking tape so
that I know when I’m approaching the centre of
the blank.
Now that you’re ready to go, review Gavin’s turning video again, mount the blank on a large chuck,
clean up the face, mark the cut lines, and let the
chips fall where they may. If coring a natural edge
bowl, it’s nearly impossible to draw lines on the
uneven bark. Put some masking tape on your tool
rest, mark the lines on the tape, then cut partway
into the spinning blank with a parting tool. When
aligning the jig on a flat blank, it’s relatively easy to
align parallel to the face of the blank, but not so
easy with an uneven natural edge. In that case,
visually align perpendicular to the ways of your
lathe.
I’ve not had a lot of experience coring bowls with
this jig, I’m still learning. Up to now, it’s been bowl
blanks in the 12” range, and I have used only the
red blade. I find it easier than trying to guess at
the entry angle, and adjusting as you go. I’m quite
sure that on larger blanks, you could use the green
or white blade for the outer bowls and red for the
inner. The marks on the blank will remain constant,
but entry angle will change when you change the
input depending on choice of blade. It takes practice to become comfortable with this jig. If you
own a McNaughton Center Saver coring system,
and would like to take my jig on a test drive before
making your own, you’re welcome to borrow mine.
And finally, I would like to acknowledge Gavin
Brunton for sharing this innovative jig and Google
sheet with the world of wood turners, and for giving his permission to publish this article. For further information on his work, and unique life style
in New Zealand, visit his website. https://
woodenbowl.co.nz/about-gavin/

Tell us about your background - how did you
get into woodturning?
I’m an avid gardener and reader and wanted to
build a book box for our greenspace on the street,
so I took the woodworking course at the West Vancouver Senior Centre. Over my time in the course, I
noticed how much fun the turners had, and it was
something that I was very interested in trying. I
took my first woodturning class in May of 2022 and
then in September took the Guilds 101 class with
Bruce Campbell.
Tell us about your workshop/studio.
It’s a work in progress! We rent and I’ve had to get
an electrician to wire a very old, uninsulated garage, redo a couple walls and put in an air filter. My
new lathe was set up and then life got in the way.
My sister passed away, and I’ve spent the past 5
months going back and forth to Seattle cleaning
and selling her home. Now my garage is a bit full
and I’m working to clear it so I can get back to turning. Thank goodness I take the woman’s class at
the Seniors Centre, it keeps me from forgetting
how to turn!
What tools do you like using at your lathe?
I love my bowl gouge and all the things I can do
with it. I also really like the skewchigouge from Lee
Valley. It’s a combo of a skew chisel and gouge.
What is your favourite wood?
That’s very hard to pick one. The first bowl I ever
turned was canary wood and it is lovely. I’m also
really loving the curly maple, as well as cherry, but I
do love walnut too!
What finishes do you prefer using?
Different natural wax blends, as I’d like my bowls
to be multipurpose and usable for food.
Do you ever incorporate other materials into
your pieces?
Not yet, I still have lots to learn. If I can, I’d like to
work some metal in with the wood as a stand or
holding piece.
What other types of woodworking or pursuits
do you have?
I’m in the process of rebuilding my book box and
have other woodworking projects I’d like to try.
Also, I have large gardens, both vegetables and
flower and spend a lot of time in the yard. Mushroom hunting, daily big walks with my husband and
our dog, and reading for my book club.

 Always wear safety goggles or safety
glasses that include side protectors.
Use a full face shield for bowl, vessel, or
any turning involving chucks and faceplates.
 Use a combination of dust mask, air filtration helmet, proper ventilation, and/
or dust collection system as appropriate. Fine particles from a grinder and
wood dust are harmful to your respiratory system.
 Wear hearing protection during extended periods of turning.
 Turn the lathe off before adjusting the
tool rest or tool rest base, i.e., banjo.
 Always remove chuck keys, adjusting
wrenches, and knockout bars immediately after use. Never leave them in
place, even for a moment.
 Tie back long hair and avoid loose
clothing, jewelry, or any dangling objects that may catch on rotating parts
or accessories.
 When using a faceplate, be certain the
workpiece is solidly mounted with stout
screws (#10 or #12 sheet metal screws
as a minimum). Do not use dry wall or
deck screws.
 When turning between centres, be certain the workpiece is firmly mounted
between the headstock driving centre
and tailstock centre.
 Ensure the belt guard or cover is in
place.
 Check that all locking devices on the
tailstock and tool rest assembly (rest
and base) are tight before operating the
lathe.
 Ensure the blank is securely fastened.
 Rotate your workpiece backwards by
hand to make sure it clears the toolrest
and bed before turning the lathe on.
 Stay clear of the areas directly behind
and in front of the workpiece, they are
the most likely areas for a piece to travel as it comes off the lathe. A good safety habit is to step out of this zone when
turning on the lathe, keeping your hand
on the switch in case you need to turn
the machine off. When observing someone else turn, stay out of these zones.
 Always check the speed of the lathe before turning it on. Use slower speeds
for larger diameters or rough pieces
and higher speeds for smaller diameters and pieces that are balanced. Always start a piece at a slower speed until the workpiece is balanced. If the
lathe is shaking or vibrating, lower the
speed. If the workpiece vibrates, always
stop the machine to verify why. As a
starting point, consult your operator’s
manual for recommended speeds for a
particular lathe. Ensure the lathe speed
is compatible with the size of the blank.
 Exercise extra caution when using stock
(Continued on page 28)

June 2024
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 28
with cracks, splits, checks, bark pockets,
knots, irregular shapes, or protuberances. Beginners should avoid these types
of stock until they have greater
knowledge of working such wood.
 Hold turning tools securely on the
toolrest, holding the tool in a controlled
but comfortable manner. Always contact the tool rest with the tool before
contacting the wood.
 Note that, when running a lathe in reverse, it is possible for a chuck or faceplate to unscrew unless it is securely
tightened or locked on the lathe spindle.
 Know your capabilities and limitations.
An experienced woodturner is capable
of lathe speeds, techniques, and procedures not recommended for beginning
turners.
 Always remove the tool rest before
sanding, finishing, or polishing operations.
 Don’t overreach, keep proper footing,
and keep your balance at all times.
 Keep your lathe in good repair. Check
for damaged parts, alignment, binding
of moving parts, and other conditions
that may affect its operation.
 Keep tools sharp and clean for better
and safer performance. Don’t force a
dull tool. Don’t use a tool for a purpose
for which it was not designed or intended.
 Consider your work environment. Don’t
use a lathe in damp or wet locations.
Do not use in presence of flammable
liquids or gases, and always keep a fully
-charged fire extinguisher close at
hand. Keep your work area well lit.
 Stay alert. Watch what you are doing.
Pay close attention to unusual sounds
or vibrations. Stop the lathe to investigate the cause. Don’t operate machines
when you are tired or under the influence of drugs or alcohol.
 Guard against electric shock. Inspect
electric cords for damage. Avoid the
use of extension cords.
 Never leave the lathe running unattended. Turn power off. Don’t leave
lathe until it comes to a complete stop.
 Many accidents to woodturners occur
while using saws, especially band and
chain saws. Learn and follow the safety
guidelines for this equipment.
For more information on woodturning
safety please visit the AAW’s Woodturning Safety webpage and GVWG Safety
webpage.
